analysis.one_liner: Gives hourly retail, food service, cleaning, hospitality, and warehouse workers advance schedule notice, predictability pay, and the right to request stable hours.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on December 17, 2025 with 20 cosponsors and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 15 or more workers to give covered hourly employees their schedules at least 14 days ahead, and to pay extra — "predictability pay" — when they change a schedule with less notice, add an hour of pay for split shifts, and pay 1.5 times the wage when a worker is scheduled with less than 11 hours of rest between shifts. It would also give every employee the right to ask for changes to hours, times, or location of work for reasons like a health condition, caregiving, school, or a second job, and require the employer to discuss the request in good faith rather than just refuse. Retaliation against workers who use these rights would be unlawful, with back pay, damages, and lawsuits available to enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly, non-supervisory workers in retail sales, food preparation and serving, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses — occupations where the bill's own findings say about two-thirds of workers get less than two weeks' schedule notice, one in five work on-call shifts, and one in three work "clopening" shifts (a late close followed by an early open). These workers would get two weeks' notice of schedules, extra pay when employers change schedules late or split their day, the right to decline unposted extra hours without penalty, and a protected right to request predictable hours for caregiving, school, health needs, or a second job. The bill's findings note these effects fall hardest on low-paid workers, mothers who are primary breadwinners, and workers of color.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly retail, food service, cleaning, and warehouse workers

how_it_helps.text: Employers must give covered employees written schedules at least 14 days in advance, and pay $75 per day for each day a schedule is not provided on time.

If an employer adds hours or moves a shift with less than 14 days' notice, the worker gets an extra hour of pay; if the employer cuts or cancels scheduled hours, the worker gets half pay for the lost hours.
Workers get one extra hour of pay for each day with a split shift, and 1.5 times their rate for hours worked with less than 11 hours of rest after the previous shift — unless they consent in writing.

Any employee may request changes to hours, times, location, notice, or schedule stability; for requests tied to a serious health condition, caregiving, education or training, or another job, the employer must grant the request unless it has a bona fide business reason, and must explain any denial.
Employers must tell covered sector employees their estimated minimum monthly hours for the coming year and update it annually, so workers can plan finances, child care, and second jobs.

Firing, demoting, cutting hours, or otherwise retaliating against a worker for using these rights is unlawful, enforceable by the Labor Department and by employees in court with double (liquidated) damages and attorney's fees.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in the covered sectors — retail chains, restaurants, hotels, warehouses, and cleaning companies — bear the costs: scheduling farther in advance, predictability and split-shift pay, the $75-per-day notice penalty, possible civil penalties of $500 to $5,000 per willful and repeated violation, and the administrative work of tracking consents and posting schedules. The bill's findings argue these costs are partly offset, citing a randomized study at Gap Inc. stores in which more stable schedules increased productivity and sales and reduced turnover, but the direct expense falls on the employers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retail, restaurant, hotel, warehouse, and cleaning employers

drawbacks.text: Employers with demand that shifts day to day — restaurants and retail in particular — would face real costs to schedule 14 days ahead and would owe predictability pay for routine short-notice changes, including half pay for any cancelled scheduled hours, which small and thin-margin operators say is hard to absorb.

The bill lets workers bound by a collective bargaining agreement be exempted from all of its protections if the union contract governs scheduling and expressly waives the Act — so union-covered workers in the same sectors could be left with weaker rights than nonunion coworkers.

Compliance is largely complaint-driven: the Labor Department can investigate and sue, and workers can sue, but a worker who fears retaliation may not complain, and the bill caps its civil penalties at $1,000 per violation for willful and repeated notice violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the benefits are concrete and immediate: knowing your schedule two weeks out, getting paid when the employer changes it late, and being able to ask for hours you can plan a life around without risking your job. The costs land on covered employers, who already must comply with similar fair-scheduling laws in Oregon and ten cities that, per the bill's own findings, improved workers' outcomes without the predicted collapse — though national rules are a bigger adjustment for demand-driven businesses. The union waiver is the clearest design flaw, allowing collectively bargained workers to be opted out entirely. On balance this is a targeted labor standard, not a sweeping mandate: it applies to specific low-wage, high-instability occupations, not all workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was just introduced in the Senate and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has not acted on it; Congress is still in session, so it is waiting.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Schedules That Work Act in the Senate on December 17, 2025, joined by 20 original cosponsors — 19 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pernels — the standard first step that puts a bill in committee where it must be scheduled for a hearing or markup to advance.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — has been taken since the referral.

An earlier version of this legislation was introduced in previous Congresses and did not advance; the bill's findings note that since 2015 ten cities and the State of Oregon have enacted similar fair-scheduling laws on their own.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet — the bill is pending in committee. If it follows the usual path for labor standards bills introduced by minority-party senators in a committee controlled by the other party, the beneficiaries of inaction would be the retail, restaurant, hotel, warehouse, and cleaning employers the bill would regulate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: 19 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, including Sens. Blumenthal, Baldwin, Durbin, Booker, Sanders, Klobuchar, Schumer, Murray, and Fetterman.

for.name: 1 of 2 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors are Democrats or Independents, and no Republican has cosponsored, but no vote or stated opposition has been recorded yet because the bill has not moved past its committee referral.

industries.note: The bill's advance-notice mandate, $75-per-day notice penalty, predictability pay, and split-shift pay directly raise labor costs and constrain just-in-time scheduling practices the bill's findings describe as common in these sectors. Their business model benefits from workers being available on short notice at no premium.
Hospitality establishments are explicitly covered by the scheduling mandates, predictability pay, and 11-hour rest rule, which add costs and limit last-minute staffing flexibility.

Warehouse establishments are explicitly covered; the bill would curtail volatile, demand-driven scheduling and require pay premiums for short-notice changes in an industry built around fluctuating volume.
Cleaning occupations are covered by the advance-notice, predictability pay, and rest requirements, adding compliance costs to a low-margin, contract-driven industry.

Union contracts can waive the Act entirely if they govern scheduling, so covered employers with collective bargaining agreements escape its mandates while nonunion competitors bear them — an odd structure that relieves the most organized workplaces of the new rules.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which is controlled by the party that supplied no cosponsors. Labor standards bills at this stage almost never get a hearing or markup without the committee majority's support, so the likely path is that S. 3550 sits in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress unless there is a significant shift in scheduling politics or the provisions are attached to broader legislation.
